falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: Registry object created or deleted
rules.plain: A process created or deleted a monitored registry key or value.
rules.why: Microsoft documents Sysmon events as observational rather than alerts. Meaning comes from the process, file, registry, or network context and from nearby events.
rules.action: Use the target path and process to evaluate persistence or configuration changes.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: Registry value set
rules.plain: A process wrote data to a monitored registry value.
rules.why: Microsoft documents Sysmon events as observational rather than alerts. Meaning comes from the process, file, registry, or network context and from nearby events.
rules.action: Inspect the target and data when it changes a startup, security, or policy location.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: Registry key renamed
rules.plain: A process renamed a monitored registry key.
rules.why: Microsoft documents Sysmon events as observational rather than alerts. Meaning comes from the process, file, registry, or network context and from nearby events.
rules.action: Review unexpected renames in persistence or security-policy locations.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: Alternate data stream created
rules.plain: A process created a named file stream and Sysmon recorded its hash.
rules.why: Microsoft documents Sysmon events as observational rather than alerts. Meaning comes from the process, file, registry, or network context and from nearby events.
rules.action: Check the stream name, file origin, and process. Browsers create Zone.Identifier legitimately; payload staging can also use streams.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: Sysmon configuration changed
rules.plain: The active Sysmon filtering configuration changed.
rules.why: Microsoft documents Sysmon events as observational rather than alerts. Meaning comes from the process, file, registry, or network context and from nearby events.
rules.action: Confirm the change matches an approved deployment. An unexpected reduction in telemetry deserves investigation.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: Named pipe created
rules.plain: A process created a named pipe.
rules.why: Microsoft documents Sysmon events as observational rather than alerts. Meaning comes from the process, file, registry, or network context and from nearby events.
rules.action: Use the pipe name and process as correlation evidence; many applications use pipes for ordinary IPC.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: Named pipe connected
rules.plain: A process connected to a named pipe.
rules.why: Microsoft documents Sysmon events as observational rather than alerts. Meaning comes from the process, file, registry, or network context and from nearby events.
rules.action: Pair this with the pipe-creation event to identify both sides of the communication.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: WMI event filter registered
rules.plain: A persistent WMI event filter was registered.
rules.why: Microsoft documents Sysmon events as observational rather than alerts. Meaning comes from the process, file, registry, or network context and from nearby events.
rules.action: Confirm the filter belongs to approved management software; WMI subscriptions are also a persistence mechanism.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: WMI event consumer registered
rules.plain: A persistent WMI event consumer was registered.
rules.why: Microsoft documents Sysmon events as observational rather than alerts. Meaning comes from the process, file, registry, or network context and from nearby events.
rules.action: Review the consumer command or script and its owner before treating it as approved.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: WMI consumer bound to a filter
rules.plain: A WMI event consumer was bound to a filter, completing a subscription.
rules.why: Microsoft documents Sysmon events as observational rather than alerts. Meaning comes from the process, file, registry, or network context and from nearby events.
rules.action: Correlate events 19 through 21 and remove an unapproved subscription only after preserving its command and owner.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: DNS query
rules.plain: A process issued a DNS query.
rules.why: Microsoft documents Sysmon events as observational rather than alerts. Meaning comes from the process, file, registry, or network context and from nearby events.
rules.action: Use the process, query name, and result as timeline evidence; ordinary applications generate large volumes of these.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: File deleted and archived
rules.plain: A process deleted a file and Sysmon archived a copy.
rules.why: Microsoft documents Sysmon events as observational rather than alerts. Meaning comes from the process, file, registry, or network context and from nearby events.
rules.action: Review the deleting process and preserved file when the path is unexpected; routine cleanup also generates this.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: Clipboard content changed
rules.plain: The system clipboard content changed and Sysmon recorded its hash.
rules.why: Microsoft documents Sysmon events as observational rather than alerts. Meaning comes from the process, file, registry, or network context and from nearby events.
rules.action: Use the event only as correlation evidence unless policy says the source process or timing is unexpected.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: Process image tampering detected
rules.plain: Sysmon detected a process-hiding image change such as hollowing or herpaderp.
rules.why: Microsoft documents Sysmon events as observational rather than alerts. Meaning comes from the process, file, registry, or network context and from nearby events.
rules.action: Preserve the process tree and image hashes, isolate the host if the process is not an approved security or test tool, and investigate immediately.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: File deletion detected
rules.plain: A process deleted a monitored file without archiving its contents.
rules.why: Microsoft documents Sysmon events as observational rather than alerts. Meaning comes from the process, file, registry, or network context and from nearby events.
rules.action: Use the process and path to connect cleanup or destruction to the rest of the timeline.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: Executable file creation blocked
rules.plain: Sysmon blocked creation of an executable file under its configured rule.
rules.why: Microsoft documents Sysmon events as observational rather than alerts. Meaning comes from the process, file, registry, or network context and from nearby events.
rules.action: Review the process, target, and hash. The block succeeded, but the attempted executable creation still needs attribution.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: File shredding blocked
rules.plain: Sysmon blocked a file-shredding operation under its configured rule.
rules.why: Microsoft documents Sysmon events as observational rather than alerts. Meaning comes from the process, file, registry, or network context and from nearby events.
rules.action: Identify the process and target. Confirm approved secure deletion or investigate attempted evidence destruction.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: Executable file detected
rules.plain: Sysmon detected creation of a portable executable file.
rules.why: Microsoft documents Sysmon events as observational rather than alerts. Meaning comes from the process, file, registry, or network context and from nearby events.
rules.action: Review the creating process, target, signature, and hash in context; installers produce this normally.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: Sysmon internal error
rules.plain: Sysmon reported an internal error and may have lost telemetry.
rules.why: An internal error creates a coverage gap: activity can occur while the expected Sysmon evidence is missing.
rules.action: Read the error text, check resource pressure and Sysmon version, then correct the failure and confirm events resume.
falsepositives: Approved administration, development, security, and software deployment can produce this event.

rules.title: Defender scan started
rules.plain: Microsoft Defender Antivirus started the scan described in the event.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: No action is required unless the scan never produces a completion or failure event.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: Defender scan finished
rules.plain: Microsoft Defender Antivirus completed a scan.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: Read the scan type, duration, and result as ordinary protection history.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: Defender scan stopped early
rules.plain: A Defender scan ended before completion.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: Read the reason and rerun the scan if it was not intentionally cancelled.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: Defender detected malware or unwanted software
rules.plain: Defender detected the threat and resource named in the event.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: Review the threat, path, user, and origin, then confirm a later action event quarantined or removed it.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: Defender took a protection action
rules.plain: Defender attempted the remediation action recorded for a detected threat.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: Read Action and Action Status. Confirm the result is Clean, Quarantine, or Remove rather than Allow or No action.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: Defender could not complete a protection action
rules.plain: Defender failed while trying to remediate the threat named in the event.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: Update security intelligence, use the error details, and rerun remediation or an offline scan.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: Defender detected a threat
rules.plain: Defender detected malware or potentially unwanted software and recorded its severity, path, origin, and process.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: Confirm a following 1117 event performed an acceptable action. If none exists, isolate and remediate the resource.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: Defender recorded the threat action
rules.plain: Defender acted on a detected threat, with the result and action status in the event.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: Verify the action was Clean, Quarantine, or Remove. Allow, None, and No action leave the threat unremediated.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: Defender remediation hit a noncritical error
rules.plain: Defender could not complete one task associated with threat remediation.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: Read the error and action status, update definitions, and verify the threat no longer remains.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: Defender remediation failed critically
rules.plain: Defender encountered a critical failure while acting on a detected threat.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: Treat the endpoint as potentially unprotected: isolate as appropriate, update definitions, run an offline scan, and verify removal.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: Attack surface reduction blocked activity
rules.plain: A Defender attack-surface-reduction rule blocked the process or resource in the event.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: The block succeeded. Attribute the process and path, then tune the rule only if the activity is approved and required.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: Controlled Folder Access blocked disk-sector modification
rules.plain: Controlled Folder Access stopped an untrusted process from modifying protected disk sectors.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: Review the process and device. Allow it only after confirming it is trusted and the low-level write is required.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: Defender real-time protection was disabled
rules.plain: Real-time malware scanning was turned off.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: Confirm this was an approved policy or another registered antivirus. Otherwise re-enable protection and investigate who changed it.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: Defender real-time protection configuration changed
rules.plain: A real-time protection feature setting changed.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: Compare the old and new setting with policy. Investigate only when the change is unexpected.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: Defender configuration changed
rules.plain: A Microsoft Defender Antivirus configuration value changed.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: Verify the old and new values against policy; Microsoft notes that unexpected changes can be caused by malware.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: Defender engine failed
rules.plain: The antimalware engine crashed, hung, or stopped because of an unexpected error.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: Restart the protection service, update the platform and intelligence, and verify real-time protection returns.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: Defender malware scanning was disabled
rules.plain: Scanning for malware and potentially unwanted software was turned off.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: Confirm another approved antivirus owns protection; otherwise re-enable Defender and investigate the policy or actor.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: Defender virus scanning was disabled
rules.plain: Virus scanning was turned off.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: Confirm another approved antivirus owns protection; otherwise re-enable scanning and investigate the change.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: Tamper protection blocked a Defender change
rules.plain: Tamper protection stopped an attempted settings change.
rules.why: This is a first-party Defender state or threat record. The event details and adjacent detection, action, or recovery events determine whether protection succeeded.
rules.action: The protection held. Identify the setting and initiating management tool or process, then confirm the attempt was authorized.
falsepositives: Approved policy and another registered antivirus can intentionally change Defender state.

rules.title: An application crash report names the faulting module
rules.plain: Windows Error Reporting preserved the crashed application, its version, the module where the exception surfaced and the exception code in Report.wer.
rules.why: This survives after the matching event rolls out of the Application log and separates crashes of the same program in different modules. The named module is the place the exception surfaced, not automatic proof that module caused it.
rules.action: Use the application and module named in the evidence to update or repair that component. If it recurs, collect the matching user-mode dump and inspect the stack before blaming or removing the module.
falsepositives: Security software and compatibility layers can appear as the faulting module because they were injected into the process, even when the application triggered the failure.

rules.title: A kernel minidump records the blue-screen stop code
rules.plain: The fixed kernel dump header contains the bug-check code and its four parameters, so the kind of blue screen is still identifiable without loading symbols or running a debugger.
rules.why: The stop code narrows the failed subsystem and remains available even when the matching BugCheck event has rolled out of the System log. It does not name the responsible driver; that conclusion needs the dump stack.
rules.action: Look up the stop code in the Microsoft Bug Check Code Reference and interpret its four parameters for that code. Use WinDbg or another debugger with symbols before attributing the crash to a driver.

rules.title: A volume ran out of usable space
rules.plain: NTFS could not complete an operation because the named volume had no usable space left for it.
rules.why: Writes can fail even when Explorer still shows a small amount free because transactions, the page file, or thin-provisioned backing storage need reserved capacity.
rules.action: Read the volume and process from the event, free or extend space there, then repeat the failed operation. On thin-provisioned storage, check the backing pool as well as the Windows volume.

rules.title: A file-system I/O took more than 30 seconds
rules.plain: NTFS waited over 30 seconds for one storage operation to finish.
rules.why: A single stall can follow sleep, removable storage, or heavy contention. Repeated stalls on the same volume point to storage latency, a saturated path, or a device that is becoming unreliable.
rules.action: Read the process and volume from the event. Check nearby disk, StorPort, and NTFS errors, then measure latency and inspect the device and storage path if the warning repeats.
falsepositives: A sleeping external disk or a one-time storage snapshot can produce an isolated stall without a failing device.

rules.title: A device had a problem starting
rules.plain: Windows configured the device but its driver or service did not start successfully.
rules.why: The device can be unavailable or left on a fallback driver. The problem and status codes in the event distinguish a missing device from a driver, service, or resource failure.
rules.action: Match the device instance and driver name to Device Manager and SetupAPI findings, then update, roll back, or reinstall that device's driver if the failure is current.
falsepositives: A removed virtual or transient device can leave an old configuration failure after it no longer matters.

rules.title: Windows could not start a packaged application
rules.plain: The AppModel runtime could not create the process for the package named in the event.
rules.why: This is the launch failure itself rather than routine package activity. The package name and error code identify which app failed and whether the problem is recurring.
rules.action: Use the package name and error code from the event to identify the app. If users still cannot open it, repair or reset that package before reinstalling it.
falsepositives: An app removed immediately after the event can make an old launch failure irrelevant.

rules.title: The computer ran low on virtual memory
rules.plain: Windows received a low-virtual-memory notification because committed memory was close to the available RAM-plus-page-file limit.
rules.why: New allocations can fail at this point, causing applications to hang, close, or behave unpredictably even when some physical RAM still appears free.
rules.action: Check the largest memory users near the event time and confirm the page file is enabled and has room to grow. Update or restart a leaking process; add memory only when sustained workload genuinely exceeds capacity.
falsepositives: A deliberately constrained test or short-lived peak can trigger one notification without an ongoing leak.

rules.title: Windows could not update the firmware SBAT value
rules.plain: During boot, Windows failed to write the Secure Boot Advanced Targeting revocation value to firmware.
rules.why: The update is intended to let Secure Boot reject known-vulnerable boot components. A failure can leave the firmware revocation state behind the state Windows attempted to apply.
rules.action: Install current Windows and system-firmware updates, confirm Secure Boot is enabled and healthy, and check whether the event returns on later boots before changing firmware settings.
falsepositives: A later boot can apply the value successfully, leaving only this historical failure in the log.

rules.title: SetupDiag identified the Windows upgrade failure
rules.plain: Microsoft SetupDiag returned a structured failure profile from the upgrade evidence, either by analyzing Panther logs or by leaving a persisted result.
rules.why: SetupDiag is Microsoft's purpose-built analyzer for upgrade failures. Its profile GUID and matched profile are stronger evidence than one isolated Panther error line because the rule evaluates the setup phase, operation and related log context together, even when LogVerdict can only read the result that Windows already persisted.
rules.action: Read the Failure and Remediation fields in the raw evidence below and follow the SetupDiag guidance for this profile before retrying the upgrade.
falsepositives: A failed attempt can remain in Panther after a later upgrade succeeds; confirm the result time and target build match the attempt being investigated.

correlations.title: The machine died within minutes of the hardware reporting an error
correlations.plain: Corrected hardware errors and an unexpected restart were recorded within the same few minutes. Separately each is common. Together they describe hardware that stopped correcting.
correlations.why: A corrected hardware error on its own is background noise on many machines, and an unexpected restart on its own has a dozen innocent causes including a power cut. The pairing removes both explanations: the component reporting recoverable errors is the one that was live when the machine went down. This is the most valuable thing correlation buys here, because reading the two findings separately is exactly what leads people to dismiss the WHEA entries as noise. Note the timestamps will usually show the restart FIRST and the hardware errors a few seconds later - that is not the order things happened in. Both are written at the next boot, when the firmware hands its error records from the previous session over to Windows, so the errors are older than the restart even though they are logged after it. This pairing is deliberately not order-sensitive for that reason.
correlations.action: Treat the hardware as suspect rather than the software. Read which component the WHEA entries name, then test memory, check temperatures and power delivery, and remove any overclock or undervolt. If the machine is under warranty this pairing is the evidence to send.
falsepositives: A genuine power loss produces the unexpected restart, and a machine that logs corrected errors continuously will have some inside any ten-minute window by chance. Check whether the WHEA rate is steady - if it is the same before and after, the timing may be coincidence.

correlations.title: An application crash took a service down with it
correlations.plain: A program crashed, and a Windows service terminated unexpectedly within the next few minutes. The order matters here: the crash came first.
correlations.why: Reported separately these sit in different parts of a list sorted by volume, and nothing connects them. The ordering is what makes this a cause rather than a coincidence - a service that died first and an application that crashed afterwards is the opposite story, and needs the opposite fix.
correlations.action: Read the faulting module in the Application Error entry, then check whether the service that died depends on it. Fixing the crashing component usually fixes both; restarting the service treats the symptom.
falsepositives: A machine shutting down crashes applications and stops services within the same window, in that order, entirely normally.

correlations.title: The unexpected restart was a blue screen, and the stop code is here
correlations.plain: An unexpected shutdown was recorded, and a bugcheck was logged in the same window. They are one event: the machine blue-screened, and the stop code in the bugcheck entry says why.
correlations.why: Kernel-Power 41 is famously uninformative - it says the machine went down without saying how - and it is the entry people find first. The bugcheck record carries the actual stop code and its parameters. Pairing them turns 'it restarted and I do not know why' into a specific fault to look up.
correlations.action: Read the stop code from the bugcheck entry rather than researching Kernel-Power 41, which will not tell you anything. The minidump the report inventories, if present, names the driver.

correlations.title: File system damage followed a disk error, so the disk is the cause
correlations.plain: The storage device reported an error, and NTFS then found structural damage on a volume within the hour. The disk failed first.
correlations.why: The usual response to NTFS corruption is to run chkdsk and consider it handled. That is the wrong response when a hardware error preceded it, because the damage will simply come back - and every chkdsk pass on a failing drive is more read and write load on the thing that is failing. The order is what distinguishes a file system problem from a disk problem.
correlations.action: Get the data off first. Do not run repeated chkdsk passes on a drive that is reporting hardware errors - check its SMART data and replace it. Repair the file system after the disk is known good, not before.
falsepositives: An external drive unplugged mid-write produces both, in this order, without the drive being faulty.

correlations.title: The update failed because the component store is damaged
correlations.plain: A Windows update failed to install, and the component servicing log recorded store corruption in the same window. The update did not fail on its own - it failed because the store it installs into is damaged.
correlations.why: An update failure alone usually gets retried, and retrying is reasonable. Paired with store corruption it will not succeed no matter how many times it is retried, and the retries are what people spend days on. The pairing changes the action completely.
correlations.action: Repair the component store before retrying the update: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth, then sfc /scannow, then retry. If DISM cannot repair it, it needs a source - a matching install image - which is the case the CBS finding in this report describes.
